overview: This file combines two clusters of State Department material concerning Japanese manufacturing. The first is a September 1948 despatch from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo enclosing American Consul Douglas Jenkins Jr.’s detailed report on the British-owned Dunlop Rubber Company factory at Kobe, including war damage, Chuo Rubber Company management, controlled raw-material allocations, black-market barter, labor relations, productivity, wages, and Dunlop’s effort to recover the plant. The second cluster, from May 1945, consists of cotton-cloth broker Edward E. I. Martin’s inquiry to Joseph C. Grew about the location and wartime condition of Japanese textile plants, an enclosed comparison of national cotton-textile exports, and an internal request that the State Department’s Far Eastern office draft a response.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 599 forwarding report on the Dunlop factory at Kobe
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards Douglas Jenkins Jr.’s memorandum on the operation of the Dunlop Rubber Company factory at Kobe under Chuo Rubber Company management.
subfiles.summary: Sebald characterizes the factory’s disposal of unscheduled surplus production through the black market as typical of Japanese industrial practice under postwar controls. He also highlights the plant’s employment of 1,200 workers to produce only half the output achieved before the war with 900 workers. The mission attributes the decline chiefly to wage arrangements based on family and social benefits rather than skill and efficiency, together with the small wage differential between labor and management.

subfiles.title: Jenkins memorandum on a visit to the Dunlop Rubber Company factory
subfiles.about: Jenkins reports on the physical condition, finances, production practices, workforce, labor relations, and prospective restitution of Dunlop’s Kobe factory.
subfiles.summary: The British-owned factory, transferred during the war to the Japanese Chuo Rubber Company, had suffered fire damage from bombing but retained usable buildings and heavy machinery; it was producing tires, hose, belting, and assorted rubber goods at about half its prewar output. Charles H. Woodward alleged that generous controlled allocations allowed Chuo to manufacture an off-schedule surplus and barter it for scarce materials outside official channels, helping supply the black market. He also blamed low individual productivity on shortened hours and a wage system emphasizing family allowances and social benefits over skill or efficiency, although Jenkins cautioned that Woodward represented the employer’s viewpoint. Dunlop wished to regain the plant without assuming Chuo’s liabilities and appeared to be preparing to resume control and perhaps establish additional factories in Japan.

subfiles.title: Edward E. I. Martin’s inquiry about Japanese textile plants
subfiles.about: Martin asks where Japanese textile plants were located and whether textile machinery in Japan and China had been scrapped for munitions.
subfiles.summary: Martin seeks a source identifying the cities near which the principal Japanese textile plants were situated. He reports hearing that much textile machinery in China and Japan had been scrapped for munitions and argues that this could strongly affect the postwar world supply of cotton goods. He encloses export figures showing the scale of Japan’s prewar cotton-textile trade and adds a personal reference to Grew’s nephew Tubby.

subfiles.title: Comparison of national textile exports
subfiles.about: The enclosure compares cotton-textile export quantities for the United Kingdom, Japan, and the United States over selected years from 1929 through 1939.
subfiles.summary: The table presents exports in thousands of square yards for 1929, 1931, 1933, 1935, 1937, and—despite an apparent OCR error reading “1945”—1939, as confirmed by Martin’s accompanying letter. It illustrates Japan’s rapid rise above the United Kingdom in cotton-cloth exports during the 1930s and the much smaller export volume of the United States.

subfiles.title: Internal request for a draft reply to Martin
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary’s office asks the Far Eastern office to prepare a response to Martin’s inquiry for incorporation into Grew’s personal reply.
subfiles.summary: The brief routing memorandum transmits Martin’s May 23 letter to FE. It requests a draft answering his inquiry so that Joseph C. Grew can use it in a personal response.

interest: The 1948 material offers a compact case study of industrial recovery and foreign-property restitution during the Allied occupation, while also documenting how controlled allocations could generate black-market production. Its account of wages, union organization, gendered pay, employer-funded union officers, and sharply reduced labor productivity is especially valuable, though Jenkins explicitly warns that much of the evidence reflects an employer representative’s perspective. The 1945 correspondence captures wartime uncertainty about the survival of East Asian textile capacity, and its export table supplies useful contemporary context for Japan’s prewar importance in the global cotton trade.
